row.name: Roman Vaults of Nuncio Viejo
row.card: 1st-century AD system of Roman walls and vaults beneath Calle Nuncio Viejo in Toledo. Part of a network that includes Roman baths and the cisterns of Delegación de Hacienda — a city built on a city.

row.name: Anta da Pedra dos Mouros
row.description: The Anta da Pedra dos Mouros, also known as the Anta do Senhor da Serra, is a megalithic dolmen situated near Belas and Queluz in the Lisbon District of Portugal [1] [2]. It is believed to date back to the late-Neolithic and early-Chalcolithic eras (4000-2500 BC) [3]. The Anta da Pedra dos Mouros, the Anta da Estria, and the Anta do Monte Abraão are a short distance from each other and are collectively known as the Antas de Belas [1] [3].

row.name: Troldborg Ring
row.description: The Troldborg Ring is an Iron Age fortification in Vejle Municipality in Denmark, 13 km west of the city of Vejle [1] [2] [3]. The surrounding area is a steep ravine known as the Devil's Valley [3]. The site consists of a raised area of about 1,700 m2 surrounded by a circular rampart [1]. One side is protected by a steep drop of 70 m to the valley floor, while the other side features a 0.5-metre-deep, 2.5-metre-wide moat [1] [4] [5] [6].

row.name: Rockbourne Roman Villa
row.description: Rockbourne Roman villa is located at West Park, near the village of Rockbourne in Hampshire [1]. In total there were probably around 40 rooms in use [1]. Of particular interest are two much-damaged Roman milestones found re-used in the building fabric of the villa [2] [3] [4].

row.name: Longovicium
row.description: Longovicium was an auxiliary fort located on Roman Dere Street, in the Roman province of Britannia Inferior [1] [2]. It is located just southwest of Lanchester in the English county of Durham [1] [3]. The fort was situated between Vindomora (Ebchester), and Vinovia (Binchester) on Dere Street, the main Roman road linking Eboracum (York) with Hadrian's Wall [1] [3]. It is about 20 miles south of the wall, and was built on high ground with clear views around the site [3]. Longovicium is also interesting in having had a copious water supply from two aqueducts, one of which was fed from an impounded source to the west [4].

row.name: Abrigo de la Quebrada
row.description: The Abrigo de la Quebrada is an archaeological site in the municipality of Chelva, in the Spanish Province of Valencia, ca. 65 km northwest of the city of Valencia [1] [2]. It shows evidence of frequent occupation by Neanderthals [2]. The site is on the left bank of a small ravine, the Barranco de Ahillas; it is a rock shelter between 2 and 9 meters deep, and 38 meters long, facing the northwest [1]. Flint tools found at the site give evidence of extensive traffic of Neanderthal populations in the area [1]. While much of the flint was procured locally, some of it came from over 100 kilometers away; knapping was done also by way of the Levallois technique [2].

row.name: Atella
row.description: Atella is not mentioned until the Second Punic War, when, although an independent city striking its own coinage, it was allied with Capua and the other Campanian cities in siding with Carthage after the battle of Cannae [1] [2]. In the 1st century BC, Cicero speaks highly of it and appears to have been its patron; it continued into imperial times as a municipium [1] [3].

row.card: Atella, an Oscan city north of Naples, sided with Carthage after Cannae. Rome occupied it in 210 BC and executed its chief citizens, yet ruins of walls, houses and tombs remain.

row.name: Nichoria
row.description: Nichoria is a site in Messenia, on a ridgetop near modern Rizomylos, at the northwestern corner of the Messenian Gulf [1] [2]. During the Helladic period it was part of the Mycenaean civilisation [2].

row.name: Massinissa Mausoleum
row.description: The Soumaâ du Khroub, also called the royal Numidian mausoleum of El Khroub and nicknamed the Tomb of Massinissa, is a Numidian funerary monument at El Khroub in the wilaya of Constantine, Algeria [1] [2]. Analysis of the objects found in it dates the monument to the second half of the 2nd century BC [1]. The finds from the tomb are exhibited in the Cirta National Museum [3] [4]. Since 2002 the monument has stood on the UNESCO World Heritage tentative list [1] [2].

row.card: The tomb of King Massinissa, who unified the Numidian kingdoms and ruled for 54 years until his death at age 90. He allied with Rome to destroy Carthage in the Punic Wars.

row.name: Pons Aelius
row.description: Pons Aelius, or Newcastle Roman Fort, was an auxiliary castra and small Roman settlement on Hadrian's Wall in the Roman province of Britannia Inferior, situated on the north bank of the River Tyne close to the centre of present-day Newcastle upon Tyne [1] [2] [3]. Pons Aelius was a fort and Roman settlement at the original eastern end of Hadrian's Wall, at the site now occupied by The Castle, Newcastle [1] [4]. Excavations around the castle keep and dredging of the Tyne yielded finds typical of Roman encampments [1].

row.name: Aves Ditch
row.description: Aves Ditch is an Iron Age ditch and bank structure running about 3 miles on a northeast to southwest alignment in the Cherwell District of Oxfordshire [1] [2] [3]. Both Sauer and Lambrick have suggested that the Aves Ditch along with the North Oxfordshire Grim’s Ditch and the South Oxfordshire Grim’s Ditch may have formed the boundary between the Iron Age tribes of the Dobunni and the Catuvellauni [1] [4] [5].

row.description: Ancient city-kingdom at modern Kouklia, home to the principal Sanctuary of Aphrodite [1] [2]. First Cypriot site inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1980 [2] [3].

row.name: Featherwood Roman Camps
row.description: The remains of two Roman camps, near Dere Street, are scheduled monuments [1] [2]. The camps date from the 1st century AD [1] [2]. They are thought to have been used by soldiers advancing northwards, and by smaller groups employed in routine maintenance [1] [2]. Chew Green and Bremenium, nearby Roman encampments on Dere Street, lie to the north and south [3] [4] [5].

row.name: The Pipers
row.description: The Pipers are a pair of standing stones near The Hurlers stone circles, located on Bodmin Moor near the village of Minions, Cornwall [1] [2]. The Pipers are approximately 2 metres high and the width between them is about the same distance [2]. They are situated about 120 metres west-south-west of the central Hurlers circle [2].

row.name: Goyet Caves
row.description: The Goyet Caves are a series of connected caves located in Belgium in a limestone cliff about 15 m above the river Samson near the village of Mozet in the Gesves municipality of the Namur province [1] [2] [3]. Homo sapiens occupation began around 35,000 years ago [3] [4]. The 35,000 year old humerus of a man from Goyet has been associated with the Aurignacian culture [3] [4].

row.name: Rough Tor
row.description: Rough Tor, or Roughtor (Cornish: Torr Garow), is a tor on Bodmin Moor, Cornwall, England, United Kingdom [1] [2] [3]. The summit is encircled by rough stone walls that align with natural stone outcroppings on the tor [1] [2]. On the southern slopes of Rough Tor, there are the remains of numerous stone hut circles, set around three or four enclosures that may have held stock [4].

row.name: Cloghanmore
row.description: Cloghanmore is a megalithic court tomb in Malin More, Glencolmcille, County Donegal [1] [2]. The monument stretches 46.3 metres in length with an oval court 16 metres long and 12 metres wide, containing twin parallel galleries divided by jamb stones [1]. The Board of Works restored the monument in the 1880s [1] [3].

row.description: Waddon Hill is a hill and the site of a short-lived Roman fort near Beaminster, in the English county of Dorset [1] [2] [3] [4].

row.name: Aglaureion
row.description: The Aglaureion, or the Sanctuary of Aglauros, was an ancient sanctuary located in the Acropolis in Athens, Greece [1] [2]. It was dedicated to Aglauros, a Greek mythological figure who was the daughter of King Cecrops and the sister of Erysichthon, Pandrosus, and Herse [2] [3].

row.name: Arsemia Ören Yeri
row.description: Arsameia on the Nymphaios is an ancient city located in Old Kâhta (Eski Kâhta) in Kâhta district, Adıyaman Province, Turkey [1] [2]. The site is near Kâhtaçay, known in ancient times as Nymphaios [1] [2]. Arsameia was a royal seat of the kingdom of Commagene [1] [2]. Apart from the Hierothesion which Antiochos himself built on Nemrut Dağı, and the second one on Karakuş which his son Mithridates II built for the female members of the royal house, a third is to be found in Arsameia, the burial site and the associated cultic area for Antiochus' father Mithridates [1] [3] [4].

row.card: Around 90 AD the Main Limes made the River Main itself a Roman frontier for about 50 kilometres. Of the many watchtowers that probably stood along it, only one has been identified to date.

row.name: Lebak Cibedug Temple
row.description: Lebak Cibedug temple, is a terraced pyramid shaped sacred megalithic site on the bank of Cibedug river near Citorek village in Banten Province at the west end of the island of Java [1] [2] [3]. The site is located on the slope of Pasir Manggu hill [2]. Square shaped terraces were constructed with oval-shaped andesite stones [1] [2].

row.name: Sweet Track
row.description: The Sweet Track is an ancient trackway, or causeway, in the Somerset Levels, England, named after its finder, Ray Sweet [1] [2]. The Sweet Track was predominantly built along the course of an earlier structure, the Post Track [1] [3]. Various artifacts and prehistoric finds, including a jadeitite ceremonial axe head, have been found in the peat bogs along its length [1] [2]. The track was discovered in 1970 during peat excavations and is named after its finder, Ray Sweet [1].

row.name: Tres Islas
row.description: Tres Islas is a small pre-Columbian Maya archaeological site 20 kilometres north of Cancuen in Petén Department, northern Guatemala [1] [2]. The main feature of the site is a group of three Maya stelae and an altar [3]. Preliminary investigations in the area of Tres Islas and Cancuen revealed evidence of inhabitation from the Late Preclassic period (c.400 BC - 250 AD) through to the Late Classic (c.600-900 AD) [3] [4].

row.name: Caballo Muerto
row.description: Caballo Muerto is an archaeological complex located on the northern coast of Peru, in the Moche Valley, in the Laredo District of La Libertad Region [1] [2] [3]. The archaeological complex of Caballo Muerto features stone and adobe constructions, with mud used as mortar [4].

row.name: Halangy Down
row.description: Halangy Down is a prehistoric settlement located on the island of St Mary's, in the Isles of Scilly [1]. The settlement complex, spanning four narrow terraces, is 50 metres long by 30 metres wide [2]. The remains of the ancient village show evidence of continuous settlement from the prehistoric to the Roman period in Britain [1] [2]. The village was made up of a complex of attached stone houses [1].

row.name: British Camp
row.description: British Camp is an Iron Age hill fort located at the top of Herefordshire Beacon in the Malvern Hills [1] [2]. British Camp is composed of extensive earthworks that have been compared to a giant wedding cake [1] [2]. The ditch and counterscarp bank around the entire site covers three hills, although those to north and south are little more than spurs [1].

row.name: Doctor's Gate
row.description: Doctor's Gate was recorded in 1627 as "Docto Talbotes Gate", named after Dr John Talbot who is attributed with improving the summit section in the late 15th century and 'gate' is derived from the Scandinavian word for road [1]. The route of Doctor's Gate was investigated in the 1970s by Peter Wroe and Peter Mellor [2] [3].

row.name: Portingbury Hills
row.description: Archaeological excavations were carried out in 1964–1965, with recovered evidence including a small flint blade 4 cm long, animal bones, flints, and charcoal, dated to the Iron Age [1] [2]. However the earthworks are too small to be a hillfort and are not in a defensible position [1].

row.card: Around 4,000 years ago Neolithic settlers came to the Niumatou Site, the oldest in central Taiwan. They left pottery and so many stone hoes that they probably relied largely on farming.

row.description: The site dates from between 5300 and 4950 BC [1].

row.name: Ballykeel Dolmen
row.description: Ballykeel Dolmen is a Neolithic tripod portal tomb and a State Care Historic Monument at the foot of the western flank of Slieve Gullion in Northern Ireland [1] [2] [3]. It is located above a tributary of the Forkhill river, in the Newry, Mourne and Down District Council area [2] [3]. The dolmen sits at the southern end of a large cairn, of approximately 30x10 metres, the north end of which also contains a cist [1] [3].

row.description: Yarnbury Castle is the site of a multiphase, multivallate Iron Age hillfort near the village of Steeple Langford, Wiltshire [1]. The earthworks at Yarnbury consist of three ramparts with outer ditches [1].

row.name: Zacpeten
row.description: Zacpeten is a pre-Columbian Maya archaeological site in the northern Petén Department of Guatemala [1] [2]. The site of Zacpeten occupies a peninsula on Lake Salpeten in the Petén Department of northern Guatemala [2] [3]. The site was sporadically inhabited by the Maya since its initial settlement during the Middle Preclassic (1000 – 300 BC) [4].

row.old_value: A dolmen called "Stone of the Moors" — a name locals gave to ancient structures they couldn't explain. Neolithic people built it around 4000-2500 BC.
row.new_value: The Anta da Pedra dos Mouros was reportedly first identified in 1856 by Carlos Ribeiro but he did not have a chance to carry out excavations until 1876 after receiving approval from the landowner.

row.old_value: At 3,600 meters on Mount Tawqaray, about 5 km southeast of Cusco, Wayna Tawqaray commands the Watanay River valley. Its position above key routes marks it as a high-altitude Inca landscape node.
row.new_value: Wayna Tawqaray is situated at a height of about 3,600 metres on the slope of the mountain Tawqaray.

row.old_value: A small cave intermittently occupied from 4000 to 2000 BC. Formed by karst erosion, it preserves layers of Neolithic and Chalcolithic habitation in tight stratigraphy.
row.new_value: The first formal archaeological excavation was carried out in 1955 by a team led by Hipólito Cabaço.

row.old_value: A Roman courtyard villa from the 1st century AD with well-preserved mosaic floors. It grew from a simple farmhouse into a sprawling estate.
row.new_value: By the 4th century the villa was now a large courtyard villa enclosed on at least three sides.

row.old_value: A rock shelter frequently occupied by Neanderthals who hunted horses, deer, and rabbits here. Stone tools and charred bones fill multiple occupation layers.
row.new_value: Flint tools found at the site give evidence of extensive traffic of Neanderthal populations in the area.

row.old_value: 3rd-century BC Oscan city 20 km north of Naples, crossed by the Via Atellana. Atella gave its name to the Fabula Atellana — an early form of Roman comic theatre that shaped Latin comedy.
row.new_value: Atella was a city of Oscan origin, one of the oldest in Campania and one of the first to have obtained the Roman civitas.

row.old_value: Guarding the north bank of the Tyne from the 2nd to 4th century AD, Pons Aelius sat on Hadrian's Wall at present-day Newcastle. Its name — Aelius's Bridge — honoured Emperor Hadrian's family name.
row.new_value: Pons Aelius was a fort and Roman settlement at the original eastern end of Hadrian's Wall, at the site now occupied by The Castle, Newcastle.

row.old_value: The largest Roman mosaic yet found in Somerset came from an eight-room villa. A mechanical digger in 2001 struck coloured stone cubes just centimetres below a farmer's field, exposing the floor.
An 8 km sandstone ridge dotted with Neolithic and Bronze Age monuments spanning 2,000+ years. A massive erratic boulder called Arthur's Stone sits near the summit.
row.new_value: Just north of the ridge summit of Cefn Bryn, there is a Neolithic burial ground, known as "Arthur's Stone".

row.old_value: Ruined quoit in West Penwith, dated variously to the Late or Post-Neolithic and as far back as 5000 BC. Two uprights and a displaced capstone survive on a moor near Zennor.
row.new_value: The quoit is situated in rough moorland on the side of Zennor Hill, at about 230 metres above sea level, and is close to several rocky outcrops.

row.old_value: Built around 90 AD. The Main Limes used the River Main as a 50 km natural barrier reinforced by watchtowers. Part of the Upper Germanic-Rhaetian Limes — now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
A 3.2 km megalithic avenue of stones linking stone circles and burial mounds, built 3000–2000 BC. One of only three such complexes in the region.
row.new_value: A significant burial cairn, known as 'Skellaw Hill', is found at the avenue's northern end, though most stones have now been lost.

row.old_value: 20-metre chambered cairn on a tiny uninhabited Orkney island, built around 3000 BC. Ancient carvings mark its stones — accessible only from Papa Westray, less than 100 metres away.
row.new_value: The main sight on the small island is the Southcairn, a 20 metre long chambered cairn dating from approx. 3000 BC on whose stones one can find ancient carvings.

row.old_value: A cylindrical limestone obelisk from the Early Neolithic with a faint spiral engraving. It was once part of a group of nine; only two survive today.
row.new_value: The Menir da Cabeça do Rochedo is an obelisk-like monument made from limestone, located just north of the town of Lagos.

row.old_value: From around 10,000 BC, Aboriginal people hunted wallaby in open tundra near Kutikina Cave on the Franklin River. This Pleistocene rock shelter helped establish the antiquity of Tasmanian occupation.
row.new_value: Kutikina Cave is a rock shelter located on the Franklin River in the South West Wilderness.

row.old_value: 8000 BC Neolithic settlement at the tip of the Karpasia Peninsula. Three French campaigns between 1970 and 1973 revealed one of the earliest known human habitations on a limestone promontory.
row.new_value: Kastros lies at the north-easternmost tip of the Karpas Peninsula, about 4 km north of Apostolos Andreas Monastery.

row.old_value: A Neolithic tripod portal tomb balanced on three upright stones. The capstone looks precarious but has survived in this position for over 5,000 years.
row.new_value: The dolmen sits at the southern end of a large cairn, of approximately 30x10 metres, the north end of which also contains a cist.

row.old_value: Maya city active 1000 BC-950 AD, one of few communities that maintained independence into early Spanish colonial rule. Zacpeten's groups are enclosed by a defensive wall with two parapets and a moat.
row.new_value: The site was sporadically inhabited by the Maya since its initial settlement during the Middle Preclassic.

row.old_value: Doric stoa from around 500 BC, seat of the Archon Basileus and repository of Athenian law. Incoming magistrates swore their oaths on a sacred stone kept within its walls.
row.new_value: In the 5th century BC, the Areopagos council sometimes met in the Stoa as well and a rope would be set up to keep people from interrupting its proceedings.

row.old_value: A ceremonial mound complex spanning 2,000 years of coastal occupation. The Huaca de los Reyes features dramatic adobe reliefs of fanged jaguar faces.
row.new_value: The archaeological complex of Caballo Muerto features stone and adobe constructions, with mud used as mortar.

row.old_value: Around 1000 AD, Kanichi blended Wari and Chanka influences into one complex: chullpas, ceremonial buildings, service centres, and a water system of wells and springs at 4,000+ metres.
row.new_value: The archaeological complex, which is about 200,000 square meters, was influenced by the Wari and Chanka cultures.

row.new_value: Porth Hellick Down is a Neolithic and Bronze Age archeological site located on the island of St Mary's.

row.old_value: Flint tools found at the site give evidence of extensive traffic of Neanderthal populations in the area.
row.new_value: Neanderthals lived in Abrigo de la Quebrada, a rock shelter on a small ravine, only from June to October, and some of the flint they knapped there came from over 100 kilometers away.

row.old_value: A multivallate hillfort on a triangular promontory, enclosed by a ditch 4 metres wide. Two spurs of a river valley provided natural defences on most sides.
row.new_value: Bury Camp, an Iron Age hillfort on a triangular promontory of Colerne Down, was built about 350 BC, yet the Neolithic and Mesolithic flint tools found there point to a much earlier use.

row.old_value: The quoit is situated in rough moorland on the side of Zennor Hill, at about 230 metres above sea level, and is close to several rocky outcrops.
row.new_value: On the rough moorland of Zennor Hill lies Sperris Quoit, a ruined burial chamber over 4000 years old. Its capstone is missing entirely; excavation uncovered a cremation pit.

row.old_value: A 4th-century BC bathing house for athletes at the sanctuary of Nemea. It sat beside the athletes' lodging and served competitors in the Panhellenic Games.
row.new_value: Thought to date to the 4th century BC, the Nemean Baths served athletes of the Nemean Games. Their circular plunge bath is one of only four in Greece; three burials were later found here.

row.old_value: An oval-shaped broch from 150 BC that originally stood on a freshwater lake island. Walls survive 4.5 metres high, and the sea now laps at its foundations.
row.new_value: Now on an exposed promontory of South Uist, but originally on a freshwater lake, the oval Iron Age broch of Dun Vulan still has walls standing 4.5 metres high and 4 metres wide.

row.old_value: Radiocarbon dates suggest presence here 22,200 to 14,700 years ago -- among the earliest in South America, though disputed. Part of the Ayacucho cave complex alongside Jaya Machay, the 'pepper cave'.
row.new_value: Pikimachay, a cave in the Ayacucho Valley, yielded some of the oldest plant remains in Peru, including an 11,000-year-old bottle gourd. Later layers held fishtail points, manos and metates.

row.old_value: A mountaintop site at 3,580 metres with cave paintings and stone burial towers called chullpas. These above-ground tombs let Andean peoples keep their ancestors visible on the landscape.
row.new_value: High on a Peruvian mountain, 3,580 metres up, Markahirka keeps cave paintings and stone tombs, and looks out over the Puchka valley to the towns of Huari and Huachis.

row.old_value: 2nd millennium BC. Bronze Age rectangular tombs at Nakhchivan, covered in stone slabs 1 m long, oriented north to south. Excavations found pottery, bronze ornaments, and the bones of the interred.
row.new_value: At the Nakhchivan Necropolises, farm work in 1968 destroyed earth graves and revealed Bronze Age rectangular tombs covered with stone slabs 1 m long, their skeletons very poorly preserved.

row.old_value: Kastros lies at the north-easternmost tip of the Karpas Peninsula, about 4 km north of Apostolos Andreas Monastery.
row.new_value: On a little plateau on the steep flank of a limestone promontory, in a very inaccessible spot, Kastros held small round houses with hearths and the carbonised remains of einkorn and emmer.

row.old_value: A Mycenaean settlement that cultivated olives and terebinth for export during the Bronze Age. At its peak it had a royal-style megaron, though it was always smaller than Pylos.
row.new_value: On a ridgetop by the Messenian Gulf, Nichoria was a major outpost of Pylos and fell in the same event that claimed the palace there. At its acropolis foot, a burial circle held 7 people.

row.new_value: On Bodmin Moor stand The Pipers, two stones approximately 2 metres high. Folklore makes them musicians, playing for three circles of dancers turned to stone for revelling on a holy day.

Around 90 AD the Main Limes made the River Main itself a Roman frontier for about 50 kilometres. Of the many watchtowers that probably stood along it, only one has been identified to date.

row.old_value: A Neolithic and Bronze Age cemetery from 3300-800 BC with clusters of round barrows. Each mound held individual burials — a shift from the earlier communal tomb tradition.
row.new_value: On Codford Down, only a bell barrow and five of ten bowl barrows survive at the Aston Valley Barrow Cemetery, where digs revealed Bronze Age and some possible Saxon urned cremations.

row.old_value: The Menir da Cabeça do Rochedo is an obelisk-like monument made from limestone, located just north of the town of Lagos.
row.new_value: On a hill just outside Portelas, the limestone Menir da Cabeça do Rochedo bears a faint spiral-like engraving. Early Neolithic, it was not funerary, and the end it served is still debated.

row.old_value: Timber causeway built in 3807 BC across the Somerset Levels—dendrochronology dated it to the exact year. The second-oldest timber trackway of its type found in the islands.
row.new_value: Oak planks laid end-to-end on crossed pegs of ash, oak and lime: the Sweet Track, built in 3807 or 3806 BC across a Somerset marsh, was used for only around ten years, then abandoned.

row.old_value: Kutikina Cave is a rock shelter located on the Franklin River in the South West Wilderness.
row.new_value: On the Franklin River in Tasmania lies Kutikina Cave, the most southerly human occupation in the world during the last ice age, with evidence of wallaby hunting on open tundra.

row.old_value: The oldest archaeological site in the central part of the island, with habitation from around 4,000 years ago. Neolithic people here knew agriculture and lived in settled communities.
row.new_value: Around 4,000 years ago Neolithic settlers came to the Niumatou Site, the oldest in central Taiwan. They left pottery and so many stone hoes that they probably relied largely on farming.

row.old_value: The site was sporadically inhabited by the Maya since its initial settlement during the Middle Preclassic.
row.new_value: On a peninsula in Lake Salpeten, Zacpeten was abandoned and resettled more than once. Then the Kowoj Maya came from Mayapan and stayed free of Spanish rule until late into the 17th century.

row.old_value: The archaeological complex, which is about 200,000 square meters, was influenced by the Wari and Chanka cultures.
row.new_value: Influenced by the Wari and Chanka cultures, Kanichi spreads over about 200,000 square meters in Ayacucho, with chullpas, ceremonial buildings and a water system of wells and springs.

row.old_value: By the 4th century the villa was now a large courtyard villa enclosed on at least three sides.
row.new_value: A farmer digging out a ferret found Rockbourne Roman Villa in 1942. Two Roman milestones were reused in its fabric, and in 1967 a pottery jar yielded a hoard of 7717 bronze coins.

row.old_value: Atella was a city of Oscan origin, one of the oldest in Campania and one of the first to have obtained the Roman civitas.
row.new_value: Atella, an Oscan city north of Naples, sided with Carthage after Cannae. Rome occupied it in 210 BC and executed its chief citizens, yet ruins of walls, houses and tombs remain.

row.old_value: An Iron Age earthwork from 800 BC running for several kilometres. Linear earthworks like this marked tribal boundaries — not walls for defense, but lines of territorial claim.
row.new_value: Once thought a Roman road, Aves Ditch is an Iron Age boundary running about 3 miles through Oxfordshire that may have divided the Dobunni from the Catuvellauni. A skull lay in its ditch.

row.old_value: A 32-km Roman road linking two forts and passing through some of the most remote terrain in the province. It connected the Hadrian's Wall garrison at Carvoran to supply bases further south.
row.new_value: For roughly 20 miles the Maiden Way ran from Bravoniacum to Magnis on Hadrian's Wall, a Roman shortcut supplying the Wall and lead and silver mines, later used as a drovers' road.

row.old_value: A pyramid of exactly 1,994 stone blocks was built over this grave in 1994 — the number matching the year. It is claimed to hold the legendary founder of the first Korean kingdom.
row.new_value: On the slope of Mount Taebak, a pyramid of 1994 stone blocks crowns the Mausoleum of Tangun, which North Korea claims as the tomb of the founder of Gojoseon, the first Korean kingdom.

row.old_value: The main sight on the small island is the Southcairn, a 20 metre long chambered cairn dating from approx. 3000 BC on whose stones one can find ancient carvings.
row.new_value: On a tiny uninhabited Orkney island, a trapdoor leads into the Holm of Papa Chambered Cairn, a 20 metre long communal tomb from approximately 3000 BC with ancient carvings on its stones.

row.old_value: 1st-century AD Roman water chambers beneath Toledo, discovered in 1628. One large arched gallery feeds three parallel vaulted galleries that once supplied thermal baths at the Plaza de Amador.
row.new_value: Beneath Toledo, the Roman Remains under Alfonso X Street are arched galleries that fed water to a thermal bath from around the 1st century AD, hidden until 1628 and rediscovered in 1918.

row.old_value: Nine-terraced megalithic pyramid on the Cibedug River in West Java. Lebak Cibedug has menhirs and altars on each terrace, plus dolmens on site, a sacred complex in Banten regency's highland forest.
row.new_value: On the slope of Pasir Manggu hill in west Java, Lebak Cibedug Temple climbs in nine terraces of oval andesite stones, set with menhirs and altars, a design older than the temples of Bali.

row.old_value: The dolmen sits at the southern end of a large cairn, of approximately 30x10 metres, the north end of which also contains a cist.
row.new_value: At the foot of Slieve Gullion, the granite capstone of Ballykeel Dolmen balances on the tips of three portal stones. Its chamber held three highly decorated Ballyalton bowls.

row.old_value: Wayna Tawqaray is situated at a height of about 3,600 metres on the slope of the mountain Tawqaray.
row.new_value: About 3,600 metres up on the slope of the mountain Tawqaray, above the river Watanay, lie the archaeological remains of Wayna Tawqaray, about 5 km southeast of the center of Cusco.

row.old_value: Porth Hellick Down is a Neolithic and Bronze Age archeological site located on the island of St Mary's.
row.new_value: On St Mary's in the Isles of Scilly, Porth Hellick Down holds at least six entrance graves. Unrecorded digs left the largest, The Great Tomb, empty but for pumice and a few potsherds.

row.old_value: Harappan site active 2600-1900 BC in Balochistan's Nasirabad District. A federally protected area between Jhat Pat and Dera Murad Jamali, occupied through the height of Indus civilisation.
row.new_value: Between Jhatpat and Dera Murad Jamali lie the remains of Judeir-jo-daro, a Harappan-period city in Balochistan once home to around 20,240 people, spread across 62 acres.

row.old_value: A 3rd-century AD summer capital of the Kingdom of Commagene, combining Greek and Persian architectural styles. A massive rock relief shows King Mithridates shaking hands with Heracles.
row.new_value: Arsemia Ören Yeri was a royal seat of Commagene. Besides Nemrut Dağı and Karakuş, a third hierothesion lies here: the burial site and cultic area of Mithridates, father of Antiochus.

row.old_value: Known as Cwichelm's Barrow, this Iron Age round barrow on the Oxfordshire Ridgeway marks where King Edwin killed Cwichelm of Wessex in 636 AD. It later served as the shire moot meeting point.
row.new_value: In 1006, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says, Danes marched to Scutchamer Knob, an early Iron Age round barrow, believing that if they reached the hill they would never return to the sea.

row.old_value: The mound at Pirak rises 8 metres and covers 4.8 hectares in Balochistan. Occupation ran from 1800 to 800 BC near two related Indus-era sites along the Nari River.
row.new_value: In Balochistan, Pirak has some very early ironwork and iron artefacts. Its excavator dates the occupation from circa 1800 BCE to 800 BCE and records three phases of unbroken occupation.

row.old_value: The first formal archaeological excavation was carried out in 1955 by a team led by Hipólito Cabaço.
row.new_value: North of Lisbon, the Cave of Pedra Furada held a communal funeral space. Among the finds: flint arrowheads, beads, a polished stone axe and a bone figurine of a rabbit.

row.old_value: A 2nd-century AD Iron Age fortification encircling 1,700 square meters on a hilltop. One side drops 70 meters into a ravine called the Devil's Valley.
row.new_value: Above the Devil's Valley, the Troldborg Ring guards a spring behind its circular rampart, likely a refuge in violent times. Its ash tells of massive fires whose source is unclear.

row.old_value: Two 1st-century Roman marching camps flanking Dere Street, the military road from York into Scotland. Troops camped here during campaigns against northern tribes.
row.new_value: Beside Dere Street, a Roman road running into Scotland, the Featherwood Roman Camps lie about 500 metres apart, two Roman camps that are now scheduled monuments.

row.old_value: Caves with 120,000 years of continuous occupation — from Neanderthals to early modern humans. Thousands of fossils document the full transition between the two species.
row.new_value: In a limestone cliff above the river Samson, the Goyet Caves yielded 99 Neanderthal bones from at least five individuals, and their condition strongly suggests cannibalism.

row.old_value: Positioned on a narrow ridge at 210 meters near Beaminster, with steep natural slopes for defense. The Wessex Ridgeway passes just north of the summit, placing it on a major ancient route.
row.new_value: On Waddon Hill in Dorset, its name Old English for wheat hill, the Second Legion under Vespasian built a short-lived Roman fort on a narrow ridge with steep natural slopes.

row.old_value: A cave with 15,000-year-old engravings showing detailed human faces with individual features. These realistic portraits challenged the idea that Ice Age art was only abstract.
row.new_value: Beside the Petit Moulin river, Léon Péricard found the paintings of La Marche Cave in November 1937, and five years of study with Stephane Lwoff revealed etchings on more than 1,500 slabs.

row.old_value: Third-millennium BC copper smelting community in Huelva, achieving furnace temperatures of 1,200 degrees Celsius. It provides very early evidence of copper metallurgy in Atlantic Europe.
row.new_value: Excavations at Cabezo Juré in Alosno, Andalusia, have laid bare the vestiges of an ancient community of workers specialized in copper metallurgy, active between 2873 and 2274 BC.

row.old_value: In the 5th century BC, the Areopagos council sometimes met in the Stoa as well and a rope would be set up to keep people from interrupting its proceedings.
row.new_value: In the northwestern corner of the Athenian Agora stood Stoa Basileios, among the smallest known Greek stoas, yet it kept Athens' laws and the stone on which new magistrates swore their oath.

row.old_value: A significant burial cairn, known as 'Skellaw Hill', is found at the avenue's northern end, though most stones have now been lost.
row.new_value: In the Eden Valley, Shap Stone Avenue ends at a burial cairn, Skellaw Hill. Its Goggleby Stone, cup-marked on its north face, led Tom Clare to suggest a Late Neolithic date.

row.old_value: A Roman fish farm from 146 BC with a connecting aqueduct carved into coastal rock. Romans engineered saltwater ponds to breed fish on an industrial scale.
row.new_value: East of Santa Eulària des Riu on Ibiza, S'Argamassa Roman Fish Farm keeps remains of rectangular tanks where garum once fermented, before amphoras carried it to all parts of the empire.

row.old_value: Maya site dated to 400 BC with three stelae and an altar arranged as an E-Group astronomical complex. A monument to Maya celestial observation, active from the Late Preclassic period.
row.new_value: On an east-facing scarp, the three stelae and altar of Tres Islas mimic the E-Group at Uaxactun, a perfect place to watch the sunrise at this Early Classic Maya capital.

row.old_value: The archaeological complex of Caballo Muerto features stone and adobe constructions, with mud used as mortar.
row.new_value: In the Moche Valley, Caballo Muerto holds a dozen ceremonial buildings on platforms, walls decorated with reliefs of snakes and cats, its people living off land reclaimed from the desert.

row.old_value: A Roman road named after a 15th-century doctor — "gate" comes from the Scandinavian word for road. It connected two forts across the Peak District.
row.new_value: Between the forts of Glossop and Brough-on-Noe ran Doctor's Gate, a Roman road named for Dr John Talbot, credited with improving its summit in the late 15th century.

row.old_value: A Neolithic ritual center from 5300 BC with scattered remains of over 1,000 people from distant communities. The bones show signs of systematic defleshing.
row.new_value: In 1996 a building site gave up bones and human skulls: Herxheim, a Neolithic ritual center and mass grave, estimated to hold the scattered remains of more than 1000 individuals.

row.old_value: Caves and stone buildings on a forested Rhone valley hill, inhabited continuously from the Neolithic until the early 20th century. A chapel from 1706, partly built in a cave, still stands.
row.new_value: Above the Rhône valley, the caves and stone buildings of the Barry Troglodyte Village were inhabited from the neolithic to the early 20th century, their chapel of 1706 partly set in a cave.

row.old_value: This Dere Street fort in County Durham was garrisoned by the Twentieth Legion. An inscription slab naming them was later reused as building material — history recycled by soldiers.
row.new_value: On high ground by Dere Street, the Roman fort of Longovicium drew water from two aqueducts, one fed by a stone-faced dam that harnessed 21 springs and stood 20 feet high.

row.old_value: Pons Aelius was a fort and Roman settlement at the original eastern end of Hadrian's Wall, at the site now occupied by The Castle, Newcastle.
row.new_value: Beneath the medieval Castle Keep that gave Newcastle its name lies much of Pons Aelius, a Roman fort whose name means Aelian Bridge, at the original eastern end of Hadrian's Wall.

row.old_value: Just north of the ridge summit of Cefn Bryn, there is a Neolithic burial ground, known as "Arthur's Stone".
row.new_value: On Cefn Bryn, a ridge in the heart of the Gower Peninsula, over sixty cairns have been found beneath the bracken, and just north of its summit lies a Neolithic burial ground, Arthur's Stone.

row.old_value: Three temples built to honour Enki, the Sumerian god of wisdom and fresh water. A natural spring inside the temple held deep spiritual significance for Dilmun worshippers.
row.new_value: Three temples rise one atop another at the Barbar Temple, the oldest from 3000 BC, thought built to worship Enki, god of wisdom and freshwater. Its most famous find: a copper bull's head.

row.old_value: A tor with a Neolithic enclosure, Bronze Age hut circles, and a summit Logan Stone. Four millennia of human activity stacked on one hilltop.
row.new_value: Rough stone walls ring the summit of Rough Tor on Bodmin Moor, once a Neolithic enclosure. On its southern slopes, stone hut circles gather around enclosures that may have held stock.

row.old_value: A sanctuary on the Acropolis dedicated to Aglauros, a princess who threw herself from the cliffs to save the city. Young Athenian soldiers swore their oaths here.
row.new_value: On the Acropolis in Athens, the Aglaureion honoured Aglauros, daughter of King Cecrops, believed to have sacrificed herself here to protect the city from invasion.

row.old_value: An Iron Age trade route crossing the Cotswolds, linking the Thames to the Severn. The Romans later upgraded it to connect their major roads Akeman Street and the Fosse Way.
row.new_value: The Welsh Way, a British Iron Age trade route across the Cotswold Hills, links the highest navigable point on the Thames at Lechlade to the lowest crossing of the Severn at Gloucester.

row.old_value: Harappan outpost on the Makran coast, occupied 2600–1900 BC, about 24 km north of Pasni. Its coastal position aligns with evidence for Bronze Age overseas maritime commerce.
row.new_value: Its name means burnt hill: Sokhta Koh, a Harappan site near Pasni, lies strewn with hundreds of thousands of potsherds, and scores of open pit ovens for firing the pottery can still be seen.

row.old_value: Two moose carved onto a rock near the river Fossen — one 31 cm, the other 35 cm. Dating to the 6th millennium BC, their position beside the river leaves them submerged during high water levels.
row.new_value: Near the river Fossen, the Rock Carvings at Eidefoss show two moose, measuring 31 centimetres and 35 centimetres, on a rock that may have fallen from a nearly vertical cliff.

row.old_value: An Iron Age village continuously occupied for 500 years, with entrance graves, field systems, and standing stones also on site. A rare intact prehistoric landscape.
row.new_value: On St Mary's in the Isles of Scilly, Halangy Down keeps an Iron Age village of attached stone houses on four terraces; digs found bronze brooches, millstones and a slate spindle-whorl.

row.old_value: A circle of 55 close-set slate stones, 26.8 m across, with a southeast entrance gap. The Lake District saw more stone circles built than almost anywhere.
row.new_value: Beside Swinside Fell in southern Cumbria, the stone circle of Swinside, also called Sunkenkirk, opens to the south-east between two large portal stones set outside its ring of slate.

row.old_value: Four tall standing stones arranged in ascending height across 13.4 metres -- the largest stone row of over 80 in the southwest. The tallest stone stands 3.4 metres.
row.new_value: Castlenalacht Stone Row, the largest of over 80 stone rows in south-west Ireland, sets four tall stones in rising height across 13.4 m on a Cork hilltop. Their precise function is unknown.

row.old_value: Herefordshire Beacon's shape is entirely determined by the terraced Iron Age earthworks, compared to a giant wedding cake. A Norman castle was added later atop this 2nd-century BC fortification.
row.new_value: Atop Herefordshire Beacon in the Malvern Hills, British Camp's earthworks have been compared to a giant wedding cake: an Iron Age hill fort thought first built in the 2nd century BC.

row.old_value: A multivallate hillfort near Steeple Langford, Wiltshire, occupied from around 300 BC. A 1991 survey found 130 internal structures alongside Iron Age and Roman coins, pottery, and human burials.
row.new_value: Three ramparts with outer ditches ring Yarnbury Castle, an Iron Age hillfort in Wiltshire. Around 130 structures hint at long settlement, and an earlier, smaller enclosure lies at its heart.
